notes:
I ran out of searches and page fetches before I could reach several sites you listed: Enduring Word, the Bible Hub and StudyLight commentaries (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit), NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, and all the Catholic and Orthodox sites. So there's nothing below from those sources, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings. The notes come from the Precept Austin Luke 4 page (I only got through verse 1 of the full page; the rest is from search snippets), Spurgeon's verse notes, Steven Cole's sermon on bible.org, and Edersheim on CCEL. Verses 14–22 have less material than verses 1–13.

**v. 1**
- A. T. Robertson: "full of the Holy Spirit" points back to the Spirit coming down on Jesus at his baptism (3:21–22). That scene shows the three Persons of the Trinity as distinct but united. (Robertson) https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-4-commentary
- Spurgeon: Jesus was full of the Spirit and still tempted. The Spirit is never given for nothing; he prepares us for conflict and gives strength to match the need. (Spurgeon) https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons-verse-exposition-luke
- Cole: Jesus lived as the perfect man, fully obedient to the Father and fully dependent on the Spirit. Being filled with the Spirit doesn't stop temptation, but it keeps us from acting on it (Gal 5:16). https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-15-temptation-jesus-luke-41-13
- Precept Austin ties this verse to Acts 10:38, where God anoints Jesus "with the Holy Spirit and with power." https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-4-commentary

**v. 2**
- Precept Austin: the devil didn't start this conflict. The Spirit led Jesus there, so Satan can tempt only as far as God allows. (Precept Austin) https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-4-commentary
- Cole:
  - The Greek suggests Jesus was tempted throughout the 40 days, with the three recorded temptations probably coming at the end, when his hunger was worst.
  - He compares the fast to the 40-day fasts of Moses and Elijah, and calls all three miracles.
  - He disagrees with the view that Jesus went out on purpose to fight Satan. Cole thinks Jesus went to be with the Father and get clear on his calling.
  https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-15-temptation-jesus-luke-41-13
- Edersheim contrasts the three 40-day fasts:
  - Moses and Elijah each failed around their fasts; Jesus held out.
  - Moses grew angry with Israel and Elijah despaired of it, but Jesus "overcame for Israel."
  - His victory was both as a perfect man and as Messiah, so its benefits pass to his followers.
  https://www.ccel.org/ccel/edersheim/lifetimes.viii.i.html

**v. 3**
- Cole:
  - In the Greek, Satan's "if" expresses no doubt; he is granting that Jesus is the Son of God.
  - Luke's family tree has just ended with "Adam, the son of God." The first Adam fell in a garden full of food; the second Adam stood firm in a hungry wilderness.
  - There's also a contrast with Israel, which grumbled in the desert for 40 years.
  https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-15-temptation-jesus-luke-41-13
- John Phillips: Satan was urging Jesus to act on his own, apart from the Spirit and the Father. He wanted Jesus to use the powers of his Sonship in a way that broke its duty of dependence. (Phillips) https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-4-commentary
- Spurgeon: Satan shaped the temptation to fit Jesus' hunger at that moment. (Spurgeon) https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons-verse-exposition-luke

**v. 4**
- Spurgeon calls "It is written" Christ's sword, and the believer has the same weapon. He paraphrases the meaning: God can keep me alive without my turning stone to bread. (Spurgeon) https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons-verse-exposition-luke
- Precept Austin: the verses had no magic power. Jesus used them to steady himself in God's will. (Precept Austin) https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-4-commentary
- Text note (Cole): the KJV/NKJV phrase "but by every word of God" is missing from the oldest manuscripts. It was probably added later to match Matthew. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-15-temptation-jesus-luke-41-13

**v. 5**
- Cole: this was not a literal view from a high point, since nowhere is high enough to see every kingdom. It may have been a vision or a vivid description. He also says "on a high mountain" (KJV) is a later addition taken from Matthew. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-15-temptation-jesus-luke-41-13
- Edersheim disagrees somewhat. He reads it as a real, outward event, not a vision, and he notes there is no other vision recorded in Jesus' life. "All the kingdoms" needn't be taken literally, much like Moses viewing the whole land from Pisgah. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/edersheim/lifetimes.viii.i.html

**vv. 6–7**
- Cole: Satan's offer mixes truth and lies. Jesus does call him "ruler of this world" (John 12:31). But only God sets up kings (Dan 4:17), so Satan's power is borrowed and temporary. Satan also hides the cost: Jesus would become his servant and his saving mission would be ruined. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-15-temptation-jesus-luke-41-13
- Kevin Zuber's summary of this temptation: "Honor Yourself." (Zuber) https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-4-commentary

**v. 8**
- Cole: ruling the nations was a right goal for Jesus. Reaching it by bowing to Satan, and skipping the cross, was the temptation. He also notes "Get behind Me, Satan" (KJV) is a later addition. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-15-temptation-jesus-luke-41-13
- Jesus answers all three temptations from Deuteronomy (8:3; 6:13; 6:16). (Precept Austin) https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-4-commentary

**vv. 9–11**
- Order of the temptations: Luke puts the temple temptation last, Matthew puts it second. Cole thinks Matthew probably keeps the original order. He follows Darrell Bock: Luke ends in Jerusalem because that's where Jesus' story will come to its climax. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-15-temptation-jesus-luke-41-13
- Precept Austin says the reasons offered for the different order are mostly guesswork. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-4-commentary
- How Satan used Psalm 91 (the commentators differ here):
  - Barbieri: Satan left out "in all Your ways" on purpose; the Psalm only promises protection to someone walking in God's will. (Barbieri)
  - D. A. Carson: the omission alone doesn't prove dishonesty. The deceit was in misapplying the verse. (Carson)
  - Reformation Study Bible: Satan turned a Psalm about trusting God into a test of God. Presumption is not too much faith but no faith at all. (Reformation Study Bible)
  - Robertson: a public leap would have looked to the crowds like the sign from heaven they expected from the Messiah. (Robertson)
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-4-commentary
- Spurgeon: Satan quotes Scripture when it suits him, but never correctly. (Spurgeon) https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons-verse-exposition-luke
- Edersheim: some Jewish tradition pictured the Messiah standing on the temple roof to announce redemption. The Gospels make that same idea a temptation from Satan. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/edersheim/lifetimes.viii.i.html

**v. 12**
- Cole: temptation (being pulled toward sin) is different from testing (God revealing what's in the heart). Putting God to the test means demanding that he prove himself. Leaping and expecting rescue would look like faith but would really be presumption. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-15-temptation-jesus-luke-41-13
- *Our Daily Bread*: Jesus would show he was God's Son by going to the cross, not by jumping from the temple. (Our Daily Bread) https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke_commentaries_3

**v. 13**
- Leon Morris: Jesus had no special resources here. He fought temptation the way we must, with Scripture. Even so, these were temptations peculiar to the Son of God, and Luke ends with Satan clearly beaten. (Morris) https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-4-commentary
- Cole: Satan waits for the opportune moment, when we are weak. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-15-temptation-jesus-luke-41-13

**Verses where Protestant teachers differ (vv. 1–13)**
- Could Jesus have sinned? Cole says Charles Hodge believed Jesus could have sinned but didn't. Cole says most conservative theologians hold instead that the temptation was real for his human nature, but the person of Christ could not sin. Cole takes the majority view. The source doesn't attach these positions to particular denominations. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-15-temptation-jesus-luke-41-13
- Spirit or divine nature? A comment on Precept Austin (the snippet doesn't say whose) holds that Luke credits Jesus' success to his reliance on the Spirit, not to his being God, which makes him a model all believers can copy. (Precept Austin) https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-4-commentary
  - Morris (v. 13 above) makes a similar point, but adds that these temptations were the Son of God's own, not typical of ordinary believers.

**Other views (vv. 1–13)**
- Edersheim lists critical theories that the temptation was a vision, a dream, a parable Jesus told later, or a myth drawn from Jewish legend. He rejects them, pointing out that Jewish tradition never pictured Satan attacking the Messiah. This is an older writer reporting other views, not modern scholarship in its own words. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/edersheim/lifetimes.viii.i.html

**v. 14**
- Spurgeon: Jesus lost nothing in the temptation; the Spirit's power was still on him. If he needed that power, we need it far more. (Spurgeon) https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons-verse-exposition-luke
- MacArthur: everything up to this point in Luke has established Jesus' credentials as Messiah. (MacArthur) https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-4-commentary

**v. 15** – None of the pages I read comment on this verse.

**vv. 16–19**
- A sermon on Precept Austin notes that Jesus stopped reading mid-sentence, leaving off the end of the prophecy. It also says the word "favor" carries the idea of grace. (Precept Austin sermons) https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-sermons
- One sermon there (author not named in the snippet) takes a dispensational view of the rest of Isaiah 61. These blessings apply to us in some sense now, but strictly they belong to Israel in the Millennium. (Precept Austin sermons) https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-sermons
- A devotional on v. 18: after the Spirit came on Jesus at his baptism, his public ministry began. (Precept Austin devotionals) https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke_commentaries_3

**vv. 20–21**
- Spurgeon: this is how to preach. Apply Scripture to the present and show how it is fulfilled in Christ. (Spurgeon) https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons-verse-exposition-luke

**v. 22**
- A Precept Austin sermon: Jesus was telling the people who knew him as a boy and a carpenter that he was the Messiah they'd been waiting for. They couldn't believe it, and the sermon ended in a riot (vv. 28–30). (Precept Austin sermons) https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-sermons

The best next pages to read are Enduring Word (Luke 4), the Bible Hub commentary pages for Luke 4:18–22, and the NET Bible notes on Luke 4. Those should fill in verses 14–22 and the "other views" section.
